I'll help you create a shortcode for social media icons that can be used in your profile section. Let's break this down into steps:

1. First, let's create a new shortcode file for the social links. We'll call it `social-links.html`.

```html:layouts/shortcodes/social-links.html
<div class="social-links">
    {{ range .Site.Params.social_links }}
        <a href="{{ .url }}" title="{{ .title }}" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
            <i class="{{ .icon }}"></i>
        </a>
    {{ end }}
</div>
```

2. Let's add some CSS to style these links. We can add this to your existing custom CSS:

```css
.social-links {
    margin: 1rem 0;
    display: flex;
    gap: 1.5rem;
    align-items: center;
}

.social-links a {
    color: #666;
    font-size: 1.5rem;
    transition: color 0.3s ease;
    text-decoration: none;
}

.social-links a:hover {
    color: #333;
}
```

3. Now let's add the social links configuration to your `hugo.toml`. Add this section:

```toml:hugo.toml
[params]
    [[params.social_links]]
        title = "Follow me on Twitter"
        url = "https://twitter.com/dbgoodman"
        icon = "fa fa-twitter"
    
    [[params.social_links]]
        title = "Fork me on GitHub"
        url = "https://github.com/dbgoodman"
        icon = "fa fa-github"
    
    [[params.social_links]]
        title = "Find my work on ORCID"
        url = "http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3759-6883"
        icon = "fa fa-orcid"
    
    [[params.social_links]]
        title = "Find my work on Google Scholar"
        url = "https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=j_1Z_l4AAAAJ"
        icon = "fa fa-google-scholar"
    
    [[params.social_links]]
        title = "Add me on LinkedIn"
        url = "https://www.linkedin.com/in/dbgoodman/"
        icon = "fa fa-linkedin"
```

4. Then in your profile card template, you can add the social links between the titles and bio by modifying the profile-card shortcode:

```html:layouts/shortcodes/profile-card.html
<div class="profile-container">
    <img src="{{ .Get "image" }}" alt="{{ .Get "name" }}" class="profile-photo">
    <div class="profile-info">
        <h2 class="profile-name">{{ .Get "name" }}</h2>
        <ul class="profile-details">
            {{ range split (.Get "titles") ";" }}
                <li><em>{{ . }}</em></li>
            {{ end }}
        </ul>
        {{ partial "social-links.html" . }}
    </div>
</div>
<div class="profile-bio">
    {{ .Inner | markdownify }}
</div>
```

You can then use the profile card shortcode as before, and it will automatically include the social links from your configuration.

Note that some icons like ORCID and Google Scholar might need additional icon fonts since they're not part of Font Awesome's standard set. You may want to include the Academicons font for those specific icons. If you want to add that support, let me know and I can help with that additional step.

Make sure the custom CV icon is recolored to match the text color of the other icons.

---

_**Assistant**_



To make the SVG icon inherit the text color, we can use a CSS filter. Here's the updated CSS:

```css:layouts/partials/custom_head.html
/* Add styles for custom CV icon */
.custom-cv-icon {
    width: 1em;  /* Match font-awesome icon size */
    height: 1em;
    background-image: url('/images/icons/icons_file-cv.svg');
    background-size: contain;
    background-repeat: no-repeat;
    background-position: center;
    display: inline-block;
    filter: brightness(0) invert(1);  /* This will make the icon white */
}

/* Ensure hover effect matches other icons */
.social-links a:hover .custom-cv-icon {
    opacity: 0.8;
}
```

The `filter: brightness(0) invert(1)` combination will first make the icon black (brightness 0) and then invert it to white (invert 1). This should make it match your other icons in color. Let me know if you need any adjustments!

_**User**_

Is there no way to recolor it to match the font? This won't work if the section changes to white instead of blue background.

---

_**Assistant**_



Ah yes, for better color matching we can use the `currentColor` value with a mask or background mask. Here's the better approach:

```css:layouts/partials/custom_head.html
/* Add styles for custom CV icon */
.custom-cv-icon {
    width: 1em;  /* Match font-awesome icon size */
    height: 1em;
    mask: url('/images/icons/icons_file-cv.svg') no-repeat center;
    -webkit-mask: url('/images/icons/icons_file-cv.svg') no-repeat center;
    mask-size: contain;
    -webkit-mask-size: contain;
    background-color: currentColor;  /* This will match the current text color */
    display: inline-block;
}

/* Ensure hover effect matches other icons */
.social-links a:hover .custom-cv-icon {
    opacity: 0.8;
}
```

This approach uses CSS masking with `currentColor`, which will automatically match whatever the parent text color is, whether it's white on blue or dark on white. The icon will now properly inherit colors just like the Font Awesome icons do.

I don't see any git output shared in your message. However, I can help you set up your git credentials. There are two main ways to authenticate with GitHub:

1. Using HTTPS with a Personal Access Token (recommended):
```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
```
Then you'll need to create a Personal Access Token on GitHub:
1. Go to GitHub.com → Settings → Developer Settings → Personal Access Tokens → Tokens (classic)
2. Generate a new token with 'repo' access
3. Save the token and use it as your password when pushing

2. Using SSH keys:
```bash
# Generate SSH key
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@example.com"

# Start ssh-agent
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

# Add your SSH key to ssh-agent
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```
Then add the public key to GitHub (Settings → SSH and GPG keys)

Which method would you prefer to use? I can provide more detailed steps for either approach.

For GitHub Pages, the way your site gets built depends on your repository settings and structure. There are typically two approaches:

1. If you're using GitHub Actions to build your Hugo site:
   - Your source code lives in the main branch
   - GitHub Actions builds the site and deploys to gh-pages branch
   - You need to ensure your repository settings point to the gh-pages branch

2. If you're deploying the built site directly:
   - You need to run `hugo` locally to build the site
   - The contents of the `public` directory need to be in the root of your gh-pages branch
   - Or if using the main branch, the contents need to be in `/docs` and your repository settings need to point there

Can you check:
1. Your GitHub repository settings under Settings → Pages to see which branch and folder is being used for deployment

```yaml:.github/workflows/hugo.yaml
name: Deploy Hugo site to Pages

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

  group: "pages"
  cancel-in-progress: false

  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          submodules: recursive
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Setup Hugo
        uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v2
        with:

          extended: true

      - name: Build

        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v2
        with:
          path: ./public

  deploy:
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v2
```

2. Then, make sure in your repository settings (Settings → Pages):
   - Source is set to "GitHub Actions"
   - Branch setting can be removed since we're using Actions

```yaml:.github/workflows/hugo.yml
name: Deploy Hugo site to Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

  cancel-in-progress: false

    environment:

      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v2

The key addition is this step after the Hugo build:

      - name: Create CNAME
        run: echo 'goodman-lab.org' > public/CNAME

No. I do have a question about the public/ dir though - should git be tracking that folder, since it is made programmatically by hugo?

---

_**Assistant**_



No, the `public/` directory should not be tracked by Git since it contains the generated site files. It's considered a build artifact that is recreated each time you run Hugo.

You should add it to your `.gitignore` file:

```gitignore:.gitignore
# Hugo build output
public/
resources/_gen/
.hugo_build.lock
```

This will:
1. Ignore the `public/` directory where Hugo outputs the built site
2. Ignore the `resources/_gen/` directory where Hugo caches processed assets
3. Ignore the Hugo build lock file

The GitHub Actions workflow we just set up handles building the site and deploying it, so there's no need to commit the built files. This keeps your repository clean and focused on the source files only.

Would you like me to help you remove the `public/` directory from Git tracking if it's currently being tracked?

---

_**User**_

What do I need to do besides change .gitignore?

---

_**Assistant**_



If the `public/` directory is already being tracked by Git, you'll need to remove it from Git's tracking while keeping the files locally. Here's how to do it:

```bash
# Remove public/ directory from Git tracking but keep it locally
git rm -r --cached public/

# Commit the changes
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Remove public/ directory from Git tracking"

# Push the changes
git push
```

This will:
1. Remove the `public/` directory from Git's index (`--cached` flag keeps the files on your disk)
2. Add the new `.gitignore` file
3. Commit the changes
4. Push to GitHub

After this, the `public/` directory will be ignored by Git, and the GitHub Actions workflow will handle building and deploying the site.
